entry.content:
Four Months In

I’m four months into my six-month fellowship at LIGO Hanford, which means I have only two months left! Time seems to be accelerated here. The days are busy, the weeks are flying by, and somehow there is always something new to see, learn, or work on.

Over the past two months, I’ve gotten to explore more of the Laser Interferometer Vacuum Equipment Area (LVEA), spend time in different parts of the observatory, and see more of the Tri-Cities. I’ve also kept digging into my research project while getting a closer look at what commissioning the detector looks like day to day ahead of the upcoming observing run.

One of the coolest experiences of these past two months was watching Cosmic Coda and getting to talk with its filmmaker, MJ Doherty, before and after the screening. The documentary started as a student film in 1985, when MJ filmed the late Rai Weiss, one of the founders of LIGO, and his lab at MIT. She set the project down for about three decades, then picked it back up to follow the detection of gravitational waves as it unfolded.

What stayed with me was seeing people I look up to on screen, in the same place where I now get to work. Some of the people in the film are the people I work alongside, and I sit in the same chairs the scientists I admire have sat in while these discoveries were made. It got to me more than I expected, and it made me feel very lucky to be here. Talking with MJ before and after the screening was a highlight, too. I’m grateful to have artists like her telling the story of this science, and the people behind it.

Group pic with MJ, the director, editor, and lead producer of 'Cosmic Coda'.

Keep reading for more updates!

Back Inside the LVEA

I’ve had more opportunities to visit the LVEA over the past couple of months, although the experience has changed quite a bit since my earlier visits. The Horizontal Access Modules (HAMs) are now bolted up, and the corner station has been pumped down to vacuum. With the equipment closed up and the detector being brought back toward its nominal low-noise observing state, the environment inside the LVEA has physically been much quieter.

Quiet doesn’t mean nothing is happening. Getting LIGO ready for observing takes a lot more than assembling hardware and installing upgrades, and commissioning means tracking down noise sources, checking systems, and working through whatever problems pop up along the way.

Of course, there is still plenty to look at during a visit!

The overpass, the Y-arm enclosure, HAM7 all closed up, the bat hazard sign, me at the new bigger beam splitter, and me with the H2 beam-tube to be sent to LIGO India.

Speaking of the bat hazard sign, it seems a bat decided to join in on the fun as we head into autumn and spooky season! One apparently made its way into the room leading into the LVEA and nearly got loose in the area. It hasn’t been spotted in a few weeks, so we’re hoping it found its way out on its own. In the meantime, I’ve learned where the emergency bat net is, just in case our little visitor makes another appearance.

Back in the Control Room

If the LVEA has been quieter, the control room is where commissioning becomes visible. It’s unpredictable: new side quests and questions can pop up any day, and priorities shift as the team learns more about how the instrument is behaving. One of my side quests was looking at different optical channels from O4, before the IR1 upgrades, and comparing them to the same channels now that the upgrade is in. It’s a fun way to see what changed in the detector.

The control room when it was quiet on a Friday, one of my favorite spots on the couch, and a thermal image of me showing how cold my nose gets under the vents in the control room!

Not every day goes according to plan, though. I was in the control room during the recent 6.7 magnitude earthquake in Panama when we went into earthquake mode, which meant the commissioners couldn’t do any more locking work for the rest of the day. Watching a whole day’s plan change like that was a good reminder that the detector is sensitive to the whole planet, not just its own site.

Up on the Roof

One of the perks of physically being at LIGO Hanford in person is appreciating just how large the observatory is. The two interferometer arms extend four kilometers each, and seeing them stretch into the distance puts the scale of the instrument into perspective.

The rooftop of the LIGO Support Building (LSB) offers a particularly good vantage point. Looking down the X-arm, you can follow the path of the beam tube as it extends away from the corner station. It’s a very different view from what you get inside the LVEA, where the focus is on the equipment and infrastructure that make the detector work. It’s also a good opportunity to take a break, enjoy the view, and get a few photos with the people who make working here fun.

The rooftop crew (Detector Engineer – Camilla Compton, Cory Chu, me, and Miranda Claypool) and a couple of views of me with the X-arm stretching into the distance.

I try not to get used to seeing the observatory every day, and moments like these are a good reminder of how unusual this place is.

Outside of Work

Of course, the fellowship isn’t all detector commissioning and research. Since August, my free time has been filled with social events, outings, and opportunities to explore more of the Tri-Cities with the other fellows.

One highlight was going to a Tri-Cities Americans hockey game. It was a fun way to spend an evening together and experience something new in the area. We also visited Marc Pirello’s house for some Guitar Hero, which turned into another memorable group activity. We love to visit the Waterfowl Habitat, where we spend time watching the geese and ducks.

A Tri-Cities Americans hockey game, Guitar Hero at Marc's house, and the geese making their way to the river before settling into the water.

Having other fellows to explore with has made the Tri-Cities way more enjoyable than I expected.

Fall Fest at Goose Ridge Winery

Another outing took us to Fall Fest at Goose Ridge Winery. With autumn arriving, it was a nice reason to enjoy some of the last warm days, enjoy the seasonal decorations, and take in the vineyard scenery. Between the hay, the fall-themed activities, and the views across the vineyard, there were plenty of opportunities for photos.

Fall Fest at Goose Ridge, the hay, and enjoying the vineyard views.

It’s been nice watching the area change with the seasons, especially the leaves. I haven’t been around trees like this since undergrad in the northeast.

The Petting Zoo

One of my favorite photo collections from the past couple of months came from a visit to a petting zoo. There were sunflowers, a cow, a ram, sheep, and a funny looking turkey.

The petting zoo, starring sunflowers, a cow, a ram, sheep, and a very serious turkey.

Labor Day Weekend Back Home

Even though I’ve enjoyed exploring Washington, I also got the chance to head back home to Las Vegas for Labor Day weekend. It was great to catch up with a bunch of my friends and spend time back home. Having the chance to go home for a weekend was a good reminder that this experience is about more than the work itself.

Dinner back home in Vegas for Labor Day weekend! I'm so happy I got to meet up with a bunch of my friends for the weekend at my favorite Japanese Curry spot.

It was a nice reset to see friends, and it made me appreciate building a routine here even more.

Two months to go!

And just like that, I’m four months into the fellowship, with only two months left to go!

These past couple of months have been a mix of getting a closer look at the detector during commissioning, continuing to work on my research, and exploring more of the Tri-Cities with the other fellows. There is still plenty to do before the fellowship wraps up, both at work and outside of it. I’m looking forward to making the most of these last two months, continuing to learn from the people here, and seeing what else I can fit into the experience.

Check back soon for my final fellowship updates!

entry.title: LHO Fellows Program – Two months at Hanford

link.title: LHO Fellows Program – Two months at Hanford

entry.content:
Two Months In

It’s hard to comprehend two months have flown by since I first arrived at LHO in June. In that time, I’ve attended a regional conference, presented at collaboration meetings, gone on a public tour with legendary Fred Raab, explored more of the southeastern part of Washington, and licked the concrete encasing the X-arm beam tube. That last one has been a joke back home since before I even got here, but little did everyone know I was very serious about this task.

This won't be in the official fellowship report. "I'm going to lick the LIGO arm" was basically my catchphrase before I left. Two months in, I made good on it. 10/10, would recommend.

Read on for the rest of the recap.

HAM7 Day

One of my favorite days this summer was getting hands-on in the LVEA with HAM7 (Horizontal Access Module 7), which houses the quantum squeezer and its crystal — it converts one higher-energy photon into two lower-energy ones to produce squeezed light, giving us more sensitivity at higher frequencies and letting us beat the quantum noise limit. More on the squeezer here.

Working in-chamber meant full “bunny suit” garb to keep our human contamination away from the detector. Once suited up, I assisted staff scientist Camilla Compton with aligning laser beams — laser alignment cards and my iPhone camera doing the work of seeing the near-infrared and green light. Only a couple of hours of adjusting the squeezer paths, but in layers of clean-room garb I’m not used to, it felt like a workout. Worth it to see one of the optics tables up close before the chamber doors closed.

Readjusting green and red beams across alignment cards in the HAM7 chamber.

The control room has its own rhythm of problem solving — and I’ve found my favorite seat in the house. Also worth noting: a snake made its way into the clean room at some point this summer, which is not a sentence I expected to type when I signed up for this program, but it happens surprisingly frequently.

Proof that the control room yoga ball is the best chair option, UNLV's first Astro Coffee of the semester on Zoom, and a small snake friend that was found in the clean room.

GWANW: Hosting the GW Explorer Tutorial

A highlight of the last few weeks was the Gravitational Wave Astrophysics in the Northwest (GWANW) meeting, held right here at LHO. I presented my home research on Early Warning GWs and hosted a tutorial built around my GW Explorer project (read about the project: GW Explorer Workshop at Las Vegas Academy). Getting real researchers to actually use the tutorial was the best kind of validation — lots of positive feedback, interest from potential contributors, and even requests to translate it into more languages. Excited to see it grow beyond the Las Vegas bubble it started in.

Hosting the GW Explorer tutorial at GWANW.

A Saturday Tour with Fred Raab

I tagged along on one of the First Saturday Public Tours, led by Fred Raab, who’s been with LIGO since the very beginning. Getting the history from someone who was actually there isn’t something I take for granted, so I showed up on a Saturday for this one. Fred told us about the installation and what’s been learned after 20 years of running. My favorite detail: the beam tubes were insulated when installed, but after years at Livingston the insulation started failing — turned out rodents had been chewing through it, and crews had to walk the 4km arms pulling insulation out by hand. An instrument that can measure changes smaller than a fraction of a proton, nearly taken down by rats. Every tour I join, I notice something new.

The beam tube, the retired winding stairs from the corner station, a closer look at the test mass excitation setup at the LExC, and capping the day off at a LIGO star party under the Summer Triangle.

Outside of Work

My favorite weekends have been exploring the Tri-Cities and beyond — the Pasco Farmers Market on a Saturday morning, and a drive out to Walla Walla for wine tasting. The fellows also made it out to Art in the Park around Richland, packed with local artist booths and food trucks.

The Saturday Pasco Farmer's Market; me in a tree I could not resist climbing by the Columbia River; Walla Walla wine tasting with (from left to right) Derek Davis, Elenna Capote, Me, Shoshana Katie Apple, and Madi Simmonds; a piñacolada from art in the park.

Another fellow and I made it out to the Boating Derby, watching car and lawn-mower racing that closed out with boats getting dragged into each other by trucks. There was also a LIGO BBQ, where I painted astronomy-inspired magnets, brought my (famous) buffalo chicken dip, and made friends with Daniel Sigg’s cat — followed by a very serious round of homemade ice cream, made with liquid nitrogen because apparently that’s just how LIGO does dessert.

Daniel Sigg's cat, outtakes from the boat derby with Madi Simmonds, and my hand-painted magnets from the End-of-Summer LIGO BBQ.

Liquid-nitrogen ice cream is the best party trick I’ve learned here. It’s also tradition to have the fellows stir, but don’t worry, we are sometimes given protective gear! Then, on a completely different night, we stopped at What’s the Scoop to satisfy our continual ice cream craving.

Liquid-nitrogen ice-cream experiment and the neon-lit What's the Scoop ice cream shop we discovered on a craving.

The fellows and Summer Undergraduate Research Fellows (SURF) students gathered for a group photo to close out the summer before heading back home for classes. I miss you all already, it’s so quiet in the backroom now.

From left to right: Me, Cory Chu, Shoshana Katie Apple, Khanh Vu, Shrey Goel, Caroline Capuano, and Miranda Claypool.

We decided to wind down here by feeding the ducks and geese along the river. I’ve never met such friendly and polite geese before.

A duck chilling on a rock, ducks in a small pond next to the Waterfowl Habitat, and the geese who were surprisingly kind.

Wildfires have been really prominent during my time here, especially over the past few weeks, turning the sky a deep orange by afternoon. Eerie to be outside in it, but it made for one of the more striking sunsets I’ve seen here.

The sun attenuating through the smoke haze.

And after Thursday dinner last week, a few of us went on a walk to catch the lunar eclipse, and we were able to see the moon slipping into shadow right at the perfect time. I’m really grateful we had clear skies to see it.

The eclipse mid-shadow, and the moment it dipped just above the house.

Two months in out of my six month stay and this experience has already been so fulfilling. As I am writing this, we just locked the Y-arm of the interferometer after pumping down the corner station for the past month. I’m really excited to be here as we continue commissioning the detector and move into the upcoming Observing Run in November. Thanks for reading and check back in soon for more updates!
entry.summary: In-chamber work, weekend adventures, a conference tutorial, and licking the X-arm — two months as an LHO Fellow.

entry.title: LHO Fellows Program – Weeks 1 & 2
entry.content:
Settling In at LIGO Hanford Observatory

My first two weeks in the fellows program at LHO have already flown by! Between orientation, meeting other fellows, students and scientists, beginning my research project, exploring the observatory, and enjoying the beautiful Washington scenery, every day has brought something new. I’m really excited to be here and to document what I learn over the next six months.

Obligatory selfie in front of X-arm at LIGO Hanford Observatory, one of the two 4 km (2.5 mi) vacuum tubes configured in an L-shape that makes the interferometer. You can't even see the End Station!

During my first week, I had the opportunity to join the Detector Characterization (DetChar) Working Group while they were visiting the observatory and tag along on several of their tours.

Around LIGO & Inside the Corner Station

LIGO Hanford Observatory, both of the two 4 km (2.5 mi) vacuum tubes configured in an L-shape that makes the interferometer. The Mid Station can be seen in white in the first two images. The End Station is visible along the Y-arm (second image) where the black line is – that is the wind fence to block the wind coming down Rattlesnake Mountain from the Southwest. The Control Room with 25+ monitors can be seen in the third image. Finally, my desk with a beautiful window view can be seen in the fourth image.

I was especially eager to see the observatory’s two 4 km-long perpendicular arms. Their extraordinary length allows LIGO to measure changes in distance as small as roughly one ten-thousandth the width of a proton, just precise enough to observe the changes in spacetime caused by a compact binary merger out in the Universe. Standing beside the interferometer that made the first direct detection of Gravitational Waves—and continues to observe the binary black hole and binary neutron star signals I work with—is hard to put into words.

A closer look inside the LVEA. The first image shows where the new Bigger Beam Splitter is located and recently installed. Image 2 shows "HAM2-E" (Horizontal Access Module 2-E) which is a ultra-high vacuum chamber housing the input optics that prepare and stabilize the interferometer’s main laser beam. The third image shows a LIGO Engineer doing out of chamber measurements in "Skinny Bunny Garb" worn to protect the ultra-clean workspaces. The final images shows the start of the 300 m Filter Cavity Vacuum Tube used to implement frequency-dependent quantum squeezing.

I’m glad I was able to tag along on the DetChar tour to see colleagues completing work on the detector before we close the doors in the next week and begin to pump-down to a vacuum state to start a commisioning phase prior to observing. The corner station of the LIGO Hanford detector contains the Laser and Vacuum Equipment Area (LVEA) which houses the pre-stabilized laser, beam splitter, input test masses, and other equipment within 2300 sq. meters or 25,000 sq. feet!

Evenings with the Fellows

Picnics, dinners, and spending time together outside of work.

The LHO community stays busy outside of work! Social events have been frequent since my arrival, and I’ve enjoyed the chance to meet the many people who make the observatory such a welcoming place. There are weekly Thursday dinners at one of the senior scientists’ homes that have been an ongoing tradition for more than two decades. I’ve also enjoyed hanging out with the other fellows, educators, and observatory controllers who have made each day a fun adventure.

Fourth of July

Celebrating Independence Day with the other fellows.

We wrapped up the holiday weekend with hot dogs, a showing of National Treasure, and fireworks along the Columbia River. I’m looking forward to sharing more about my research project and my time here. Thanks for reading and stay tuned!
entry.summary: My first two weeks as a Fellow at LIGO Hanford Observatory!

entry.title: Valley of Fire State Park – Star Party

link.title: Valley of Fire State Park – Star Party

entry.content:
The inaugural Astronomy in the Park Stargazing Event at Valley of Fire State Park brought together astronomy enthusiasts from across Southern Nevada for an evening of science, public outreach, and observing under some of the region’s darkest skies.

Hosted by the Las Vegas Astronomical Society in the park’s new Visitor Center, the event featured presentations, telescope observing, and discussions about current discoveries in astronomy and astrophysics.

I was honored to serve as the guest speaker, presenting an overview of Gravitational-Wave (GW) astronomy and highlighting recent results from the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Collaboration. Following the presentation, attendees had the opportunity to ask questions and participate in the evening’s observing activities.

Scenes from my presentation on Gravitatioinal-Waves and recent Collaboration updates at the Valley of Fire State Park's new Visitor Center.

My presentation introduced attendees to the emerging field of GW astronomy, beginning with the fundamental concepts behind Einstein’s theory of General Relativity and the nature of gravitational waves. I discussed how observatories such as LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detect these tiny distortions of spacetime and how these observations have opened a new window onto the Universe.

The talk also highlighted several recent results from the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Collaboration, including ongoing efforts to test General Relativity, study intermediate massive black holes, and potential binary neutron star events through gravitational-wave observations. Audience members asked thoughtful questions throughout the presentation, leading to engaging discussions about the future of multi-messenger astronomy and the scientific discoveries that may lie ahead.

Short clip from the event showing a video of GWs exaggeratingly distorting Earth as they pass by.

An unexpected highlight of the evening was the opportunity to be interviewed by Noriko Carroll of the Las Vegas Japan Times. Her article covering the event highlighted the importance of public astronomy outreach and the growing interest in dark-sky education throughout Southern Nevada. Screenshots from the article can be viewed below.

Screenshots from the Las Vegas Japan Times covering the Star Party event. I was honored to be interviewed by Noriko Carroll, who wrote the article, and featured my talk. Thank you to Keith Caceres for capturing these screenshots from the article.

“A highlight of the evening was a lecture by Rachel R. Langgin, an Astronomy PhD student at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas and a member of the LIGO Scientific Collaboration. Langgin studies black holes and neutron stars through gravitational waves-ripples in spacetime first directly detected in 2015 by the LIGO observatories. During her presentation, Langgin explained how gravitational waves allow scientists to observe some of the most energetic events in the universe, including the merger of black holes more than a billion light- years away. She also discussed recent discoveries suggesting that black holes may grow through repeated mergers, creating what she described as a possible ‘family tree’ of black holes.”

“The lively question-and-answer session continued long after the lecture ended. Langgin encouraged students to pursue research opportunities, write about what they learn, and stay committed to their interests despite challenges in research funding. Her enthusiasm for science left a lasting impression on attendees.”

I was honored to have my presentation featured alongside coverage of the inaugural Star Party and the efforts of the Las Vegas Astronomical Society to connect the public with science and astronomy.

I’m very grateful to the organizers, volunteers, park staff, and attendees who helped make the event such a success, and I would especially like to thank Noriko Carroll and the Las Vegas Japan Times for helping share the experience with an even wider audience. I look forward to future opportunities with the Las Vegas Astronomical Society to support astronomy outreach and science communication throughout Nevada.
entry.summary: I was invited as the guest speaker for the inaugural Astronomy in the Park Stargazing Event hosted by the Las Vegas Astronomical Society at Valley of Fire State Park's new Visitor Center. During the event, I shared insights into gravitational waves and recent publications from the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Collaboration.

entry.title: Winter & Spring 2026 | Research Presentations & Conference Highlights

link.title: Winter & Spring 2026 | Research Presentations & Conference Highlights

entry.content:
Winter and Spring 2026 turned into the busiest stretch of graduate school I’ve experienced so far. Between local symposiums, national conferences, and university research competitions, I had the opportunity to present my work on Gravitational-Wave (GW) astronomy to a wide range of audiences—from fellow students and faculty to researchers working across GW astrophysics and graduate colleagues.

Over the course of the semester, I presented research on waveform systematics in next-generation GW detectors, early-warning alerts for electromagnetic follow-up observations, and science communication through computational education initiatives. Each event offered a different perspective on the broader GW community and highlighted the collaborative nature of modern astrophysics.

Here’s a look back at a semester spent sharing research, learning from colleagues, and exploring some incredible scientific meetings.

Gravitational Wave Physics and Astronomy Workshop 2025 (GWPAW) at Georgia Tech

Gravitational Wave Physics and Astronomy Workshop 2025 (GWPAW) at Georgia Tech Group Photo. Pictured ninth row, first on the right.

My presentation focused on evaluating waveform accuracy for next-generation GW observatories such as Cosmic Explorer and the Einstein Telescope. As detector sensitivities improve, waveform modeling errors that are currently negligible may become significant sources of systematic uncertainty. I presented recent comparisons between state-of-the-art waveform models and discussed how these differences could influence parameter estimation for future detections.

Beyond the scientific program, GWPAW provided an excellent opportunity to connect with researchers across the GW community. The workshop’s focus on GWs fostered meaningful discussions about detector development, waveform modeling, and the challenges that lie ahead as the field prepares for the next-generation of observatories.

American Physical Society (APS) Global Physics Summit 2026

The APS Global Physics Summit was a particular highlight of the semester because I had the opportunity to present two very different aspects of my work.

Presentation images from APS Global Physics Summit (Denver, CO) 2026.

My first presentation was delivered through the Forum on Outreach and Engaging the Public (FOEP), where I shared GW Explorer: A Beginner’s Guide, a computational outreach curriculum designed to introduce high school students to GW astronomy through interactive Python notebooks. The project combines foundational physics concepts with hands-on data analysis activities, giving students an opportunity to engage directly with real GW science. Presenting this work to a community focused on physics outreach and education sparked valuable conversations about expanding access to computational astrophysics education.

Later in the conference, I presented research from my Early Warning project, which investigates how GW signals can be identified before merger to provide advance notice for electromagnetic observatories. I demonstrated how early-warning signals have the potential to improve coordinated multi-messenger observations by giving telescopes additional time to prepare for transient events.

Discussing both projects at APS provided broader audience perspectives and generated feedback that informed ongoing progress of these works.

Denver was a beautiful and fun city to visit! We got to see rain, snow, and sunshine all in three days.

Nevada Center for Astrophysics (NCfA) Symposium 2026

The Nevada Center for Astrophysics Symposium provided a chance to share my research closer to home while engaging with the growing astrophysics community across Nevada.

Presentation images at the Nevada Center for Astrophysics (NCfA) Symposium 2026.

The symposium featured presentations from faculty, students, and collaborators working on topics ranging from stellar astrophysics and cosmology to GW astronomy and multi-messenger science. These regional meetings often lead to some of the most productive discussions because they bring together researchers with diverse expertise who are building long-term collaborations.

UNLV Annual Graduate & Professional Student Research Forum 2026

My podium talk featuring research on leveraging the early warning GW signal for electromagnetic observations received 1st place in my talk session at the 2026 UNLV GPSA Research Forum.

The semester concluded with the UNLV Annual Graduate & Professional Student Research Forum, a university-wide showcase of graduate scholarship and creative activity. I presented a podium talk on my research investigating the use of early-warning GW signals to support electromagnetic follow-up observations.

I was honored to receive first place in my presentation session. The recognition was especially meaningful because the forum brings together graduate researchers from a wide range of disciplines, requiring presenters to communicate specialized research to a broader academic audience. The experience reinforced the importance of scientific communication and provided a rewarding conclusion to an exceptionally busy semester of conferences.

Across GWPAW, APS, NCfA, and the UNLV research forum, this semester I presented work ranging from waveform studies and early-warning GW signals to outreach through GW Explorer. These opportunities were supported in part by travel funding, including APS FOEP support and GPSA support, which helped make this set of presentations possible.
entry.summary: Winter & Spring 2026 took me from Las Vegas to Atlanta to Denver, presenting research at the NCfA Multi-Messenger Symposium, the Gravitational-Wave Physics and Astronomy Workshop 2025 (GWPAW), the APS Global Physics Summit, and the UNLV GPSA Research Forum. Here's a recap of the busiest semester in grad school yet!

entry.title: GW Explorer Workshop at Las Vegas Academy

link.title: GW Explorer Workshop at Las Vegas Academy

entry.content:
On November 5, 2025, the GW Explorer Volunteer Crew of UNLV Astronomy PhD students hosted an afterschool Gravitational-Wave Workshop at the Las Vegas Academy of the Arts, led by Mrs. Teresa Prezgay’s advanced mathematics students. The workshop introduced students to Gravitational-Wave science through interactive Jupyter Notebooks, a tabletop interferometer demonstration, and discussions about how math connects to astrophysics.

The GW Explorer Project is designed to make Gravitational-Wave astronomy accessible to students at the high school and early undergraduate level. By combining hands-on experiments with interactive Jupyter notebooks, the project helps students build intuition about how detectors like LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA measure distortions in spacetime caused by the merger of compact binary objects.

Workshop Highlights

The workshop began with introductions from the volunteer crew and a short mini-lecture on astronomical concepts the students would be dealing with in the notebooks, like stars and black holes.

The GW Explorer Volunteer Crew introducing themselves to the class.
Group photo of the GW Explorer crew and Las Vegas Academy students.

Students explored GW Explorer Notebook 1 (NB1) — an interactive activity that brings Einstein’s ideas about spacetime, gravity, and black holes to life. With guidance from volunteers, the students discovered how these concepts combine to produce Gravitational-Waves, using interactive Python widgets that let them experiment with the underlying equations themselves.

Madeline Overton guiding a student through Gravitational-Wave simulations.
Leah Green introducing the GW Explorer NB1 notebook to students.
Discussing binary black holes and Gravitational-Wave signals.
Volunteers helping students interpret signals and patterns in the data.
Madeline Overton and Ted Johnson assisting during the workshop.

Binary Black Holes in Action

The first notebook session concluded with an interactive visualization of a binary black hole inspiral, explaining how Gravitational-Wave signals evolve as two massive objects merge.

A student exploring the GW Explorer binary black hole animation after completing NB1.

After experiencing the binary black hole animation, students dove into hands-on experiments with the tabletop interferometer, observing how Gravitational-Waves cause tiny, measurable shifts in distance. Volunteers guided them step by step, linking theory from NB1 to real-world physics.

Using the wave nature of light, the interferometer splits a laser beam into two paths that reflect back and overlap, forming an interference pattern–the superposition of combined light waves. When one path changes length by even a fraction of a wavelength, the pattern shifts revealing changes in distance. This simple setup demonstrates the same principle used by LIGO–the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory–to detect Gravitational-Waves from merging black holes billions of light-years away.

Students experimenting with the tabletop interferometer setup.
Hands-on exploration of how Gravitational-Waves change measurable distances that can be detected through light.
Volunteers explaining how light interference can reveal tiny displacements.

This particular workshop held a special meaning: the class was taught by Mrs. Teresa Prezgay, who also happened to be my former calculus teacher at Las Vegas Academy. Years ago, I gave my first math-related presentation in her class—on astrophysics—after a simple online search for “careers that use math.” I recently found the presentation that showed how to calculate the orbits of the Earth and Moon by using Kepler’s Third Law. That small assignment set me on the path toward astrophysics in college and, eventually, Gravitational-Wave research today.

Now, one of her current students, Bradlee Tejeda, volunteered with the GW research group at UNLV collaborating on designing this interactive notebook series. Watching Bradlee help lead the same kind of classroom activity that once inspired me was a reminder of how mentorship and curiosity can be extremely rewarding. We were thrilled to hear that the class enjoyed the experience so much that we’ve been invited back for another session in February!

Explore the Project

You can explore the GW Explorer: A Beginner’s Guide project at rachellanggin.com/tutorials!

These resources are open for educators, students, and outreach groups interested in bringing Gravitational-Wave science into the classroom. If you’re interested in hosting a workshop at your school or institution, please contact me at langgin@unlv.nevada.edu.

I’m grateful to Las Vegas Academy, Mrs. Prezgay, and the GW Explorer Volunteer Crew: Leah Green, Madeline Overton, Ted Johnson, and Bradlee Tejeda—for making this event possible and for helping expand access to Gravitational-Wave education.
entry.summary: Our GW Explorer volunteer crew led a hands-on Gravitational-Wave workshop at Las Vegas Academy, connecting math and astrophysics for the next generation of students.

entry.title: LVAS August 2025 Monthly Meeting
entry.content:
Following last year’s September meeting, I was delighted to be invited back by Mig Ponce (President of LVAS) and Keith Caceres (LVAS Event Director) to give an invited talk at the Dale Etheridge Planetarium, College of Southern Nevada, for the Las Vegas Astronomical Society’s August Monthly Meeting.

My presentation, “Astrophysical Implications of Next-Generation Gravitational-Wave Observations,” explored how instruments like Cosmic Explorer and Einstein Telescope will expand our view of compact object mergers across cosmic history—revealing new populations of black holes and neutron stars, and transforming our understanding of the dynamic, multi-messenger universe.

Dale Etheridge Planetarium at the College of Southern Nevada

Images from the August 2025 LVAS meeting.

After sharing key insights on the astrophysical implications of next-generation Gravitational-Wave detectors, here’s a brief highlight from my presentation. In this 2-minute clip, I introduce my Gravitational Waveform Accuracy Project—a cosmic puzzle exploring how subtle distortions in waveforms can affect our understanding of merging black holes and neutron stars.

Short clip from the event introducing my Gravitational Waveform Accuracy Project—think of it as a cosmic puzzle: what if the waveforms used to decode binary black hole mergers were inaccurate–slightly overlapped or mishaped? The overall picture would become distorted and biased.

Full Recording (Zoom)

A recording of the full presentation is available below:

Watch my full LVAS August 2025 presentation above. Thank you to everyone who made the event possible!

Video Description:
Recorded via Zoom during the Las Vegas Astronomical Society August 2025 Monthly Meeting, this talk features Rachel Langgin, Ph.D. student at UNLV, presenting “Astrophysical Implications of Next-Generation Gravitational-Wave Observations.”

Topics include next-generation detectors (Cosmic Explorer, Einstein Telescope, LISA), multi-messenger Gravitational-Wave astronomy, and early-warning detection research.

It was a pleasure reconnecting with familiar LVAS members and meeting new faces passionate about high-energy astrophysics and Gravitational-Wave science. The evening included lively discussion about the challenges of next-generation detector design, population modeling, and how Gravitational-Wave astronomy intersects with traditional observation methods to enable multi-messenger astrophysics.

Toward the end of the event, I had the opportunity to speak with a prospective astronomy student and her mother about studying astrophysics at UNLV and pursuing careers in gravitational-wave research—one of the most rewarding moments of the night.

Sharing my experience in astrophysics and research pathways with a prospective student and her mother.

Engaging with the local astronomy community remains one of the most rewarding parts of my research journey—I’m deeply grateful for LVAS’s continued enthusiasm and support for Gravitational-Wave science in Las Vegas.
entry.summary: I was honored to be invited back to the Las Vegas Astronomical Society’s Monthly Meeting at the Dale Etheridge Planetarium to present on the Astrophysical Implications of Next-Generation Gravitational-Wave Observations.

entry.title: Dark Skies in the Spring Mountains – Star Party

link.title: Dark Skies in the Spring Mountains – Star Party

entry.content:
On the evening of July 26, I had the pleasure of participating in the Dark Skies in the Spring Mountains – Star Party , hosted by Mt. Charleston, Sierra Forever, and the U.S. Forest Service at the Spring Mountains Visitor Gateway. The event reached full capacity, with over 100 attendees gathering for a night of astronomy education, public science, and stargazing under some of the darkest skies in Southern Nevada. It was a pleasure to be invited back for a second year in a row for this stargazing event. Below are some images from the presentation captured by LVAS organizer, Keith Caceres.

As part of the evening’s programming, I gave a public talk introducing the audience to Gravitatioinal-Waves—disturbances in the fabric of spacetime produced by accelerating massive objects such as black holes and neutron stars. I discussed how ground-based observatories like LIGO and Virgo detect these distortions, allowing us to study some of the universe’s most extreme events in entirely new ways. I explained how Gravitatioinal-Wave astronomy complements electromagnetic observations by enabling us to detect phenomena that would otherwise remain invisible, and highlighted the future of multi-messenger astrophysics—including coordinated observations with space-based telescopes like Fermi and Swift.

Scenes from my presentation on Gravitatioinal-Waves and dark skies in the Spring Mountains Visitor Gateway Amphitheater.

In addition to outlining the broader field, I shared a bit about my own research on constraining Gravitatioinal-Wave waveform models to better extract physical parameters from detected signals, and my current work on an early-warning project focused on identifying neutron star mergers before they coalesce.

After the talk, I handed out copies of my short Gravitatioinal-Wave comic book I created. Designed for a general audience, it uses illustration and narrative to explain Gravitatioinal-Waves and next-generation Gravitatioinal-Wave observatories. (A short video of this moment is available below.)

Short clip from the event handing out my comic book on Gravitatioinal-Waveforms.

Attendees then joined guided stargazing sessions, led by volunteers from the Las Vegas Astronomical Society, who generously brought telescopes to share views of open clusters and dense regions of the Milky Way. The evening also featured campfire s’mores, which helped keep spirits high and conversations going late into the evening.

It was energizing to see such a diverse audience engaged in conversations about black holes, time, and the nature of the universe. Several attendees asked thoughtful questions about Gravitatioinal-Waves, observatories, and careers in science—highlighting the value of accessible, community-based events like this one.

The evening included my science talk, stargazing booths, and s'mores around a campfire.

I’m grateful to Go Mt. Charleston, the U.S. Forest Service, the Las Vegas Astronomical Society, and all the volunteers who made this event possible. It was a rewarding opportunity to share current research, build connections, and support the continued protection of Nevada’s natural dark skies.
entry.summary: I was invited back for the second year as a guest speaker at the Dark Skies Stargazing Event hosted by the Las Vegas Astronomical Society at Mount Charleston. This year, I shared insights into Gravitatioinal-Waves and my current research.

entry.title: Back-to-School “Out of This World” Event
entry.content:
On July 23, I joined MGM Group’s annual Back-to-School “Out of This World” event held in the Vista Ballroom at the Flamingo Hotel on the Las Vegas Strip. Organized by MGM Resorts’ community engagement team, the event brought together local organizations and families for a day of interactive science and educational activities designed to celebrate the upcoming school year through the lens of space exploration.

As a representative of the Nevada Center for Astrophysics and UNLV Department of Physics and Astronomy, I hosted a table with my collegues sharing information about Gravitational-Waves, space science, and physics opportunities at UNLV. With support from my APS Forum on Early Career Scientists (FOEP) Mini-Grant, I provided custom stickers and outreach materials for students and families. I also partnered with the UNLV Admissions Office to offer prospective-student resources and UNLV-themed giveaways.

Scenes from the MGM “Out of This World” Back-to-School event at the Flamingo Las Vegas.

A highlight of the day was sharing my tabletop interferometer demonstration, which allowed students to see how laser interference patterns change in real time—offering a simple introduction to the same principles behind LIGO’s Gravitational-Wave detectors. I also distributed copies of my short comic book on Gravitational-Waves, which uses storytelling and art to introduce the concept of spacetime ripples and next-generation observatories.

Short clip from the event showing the UNLV Physics and Astronomy booth.

Throughout the event, families engaged with UNLV’s materials, asked thoughtful questions about space and physics, and shared enthusiasm for astronomy and science education. The interactive booths, games, and themed activities made for an inspiring afternoon of community engagement and outreach.

I’m deeply grateful to MGM Group and the organizers for inviting our research group to share Gravitational-Wave science with local students and families. Events like this are a wonderful reminder of how science outreach can spark curiosity, connect communities, and inspire the next generation of scientists.
entry.summary: I participated in MGM Group’s “Out of This World” Back-to-School event, sharing Gravitational-Wave science and hands-on demonstrations with local students and families.

entry.title: Save The Night Star Party – Save Red Rock Canyon

link.title: Save The Night Star Party – Save Red Rock Canyon

entry.content:
On a clear, moonless night in Red Rock Canyon, I had the honor of serving as the invited speaker for Save the Night hosted by Save Red Rock organization and the Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area, a public stargazing event focused on protecting dark skies and nocturnal ecosystems. The evening brought together scientists, conservationists, and the local community under the stars for a night of learning and exploration.

The event featured a constellation tour and telescope viewing, with support from the Las Vegas Astronomical Society, The Brett Torino Foundation, and Dark Sky International.

My presentation introduced Gravitational-Wave astronomy to a broad audience—explaining how spacetime ripples from merging black holes and neutron stars are detected here on Earth. I shared my current research on early-warning signals from binary neutron star mergers that enable telescopes to observe these events in real time. While light pollution doesn’t interfere with Gravitational-Wave detectors themselves, it does impact our ability to follow up these signals with telescopes, making dark sky preservation essential for the full exploration of multi-messenger astrophysics.

Stargazing, Gravitational-Wavess, and dark sky advocacy came together in a night of science and community at Red Rock Canyon.

Thanks to the Las Vegas Astronomical Society, attendees explored constellations and planets through dozens of telescopes. With beautiful weather and standing-room-only crowds during my talks, it was a powerful reminder of how deeply people care about both the night sky and scientific discovery.

After the presentation, I also distributed copies of my short comic book on Gravitational-Waves, which uses storytelling and art to introduce the concept of spacetime ripples and next-generation observatories.

You can watch my presentation above. Thank you to Nataniel Stepniewski for the recording.

I’m incredibly grateful to Save Red Rock, the Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area, and the many volunteers and organizations who made this event possible.

Our June stargazing event will be at Red Rock Canyon Visitor Center on *Sunday* June 22nd. Must arrive before presentation in amphitheater at 8:30 PM — given by UNLV Astronomy PhD Candidate Rachel Langgin. She’ll discuss how Gravitational-Wave science allows us to observe merging pairs of black holes and neutron stars — immediately followed by night sky constellation tour.
